# A router you can exercise {#a-router-you-can-exercise}


Create a router, install its middleware, then add routes. A chi router implements `http.Handler`, so Go's ordinary HTTP server and test tools work with it.

```go
package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "github.com/go-chi/chi/v5"
    "github.com/go-chi/chi/v5/middleware"
)

func main() {
    r := chi.NewRouter()
    r.Use(middleware.RequestID)
    r.Get("/hello/{name}", func(w http.ResponseWriter, req *http.Request) {
        fmt.Fprintf(w, "Hello, %s\n", chi.URLParam(req, "name"))
    })
    http.ListenAndServe(":8080", r)
}
```

`NewRouter` returns a `*Mux`; `Get` installs one method and path; `URLParam` retrieves the named path component after routing. Query parameters still come from `req.URL.Query()`. Middleware added with `Use` runs before the matching handler.


## Run this guide's examples {#run-this-guides-examples}


Clone the [guide repository](https://github.com/nnyydct-ship-it/chi-field-guide), then:

```sh
node scripts/fetch-upstream.mjs
cd examples
go test -v ./...
```

The fetch script checks out the pinned chi commit. The examples use a local Go module replacement so they exercise that checkout, rather than an unrecorded newer release. They cover path and method matching, explicit and implicit HEAD routes, middleware nesting, a late `Use`, and a cooperative timeout.

The simple server above is an introduction. The checked examples are in `examples/recipes_test.go`; see [reproduce](/chi-field-guide/reproduce.html) for their exact environment and the documentation build.

# Paths, methods and HEAD {#paths-methods-and-head}


Registering `GET /items/{id}` does not register every method on that path. A missing path returns 404 by default. A recognized path with an unsupported method returns 405. Use `NotFound` and `MethodNotAllowed` when those responses need an application-specific body.

```go
r := chi.NewRouter()
r.Get("/items/{id}", func(w http.ResponseWriter, req *http.Request) {
    fmt.Fprint(w, chi.URLParam(req, "id"))
})
```

The guide checks `GET /items/42`, `POST /items/42` and `GET /missing` separately. A successful parameter lookup does not prove the method fallback is correct.


## An implicit HEAD route {#an-implicit-head-route}


If a handler can serve both GET and HEAD, install `middleware.GetHead` before the routes:

```go
r := chi.NewRouter()
r.Use(middleware.GetHead)
r.Get("/items/{id}", handler)
```

`GetHead` looks for an explicit HEAD match first. When there is none, it chooses the GET route while preserving the request's HEAD method. An explicitly registered `Head` handler takes priority. The tests use a real local HTTP server and verify that a HEAD response has no body; testing only a response recorder would miss the HTTP server's role in suppressing it.


## Compose a subtree {#compose-a-subtree}


Use `Route` to create a subrouter with a path prefix. Use `Mount` to attach an existing `http.Handler`. Keep a trailing slash intentional: chi does not silently make every path with and without a slash equivalent. `RedirectSlashes` and `StripSlashes` are separate middleware choices.

The exact declarations are in the Go API tab: `Router`, `Mux.Get`, `Mux.Head`, `Mux.Route`, `Mux.Mount`, `Mux.NotFound`, `Mux.MethodNotAllowed`, `URLParam`, and `middleware.GetHead`. [Source map](/chi-field-guide/source-map.html) links them to the pinned implementation.

# Put middleware at the scope it needs {#put-middleware-at-the-scope-it-needs}


Install router-wide middleware with `Use` before registering any route. Chi builds the router's handler chain when routes are registered; calling `Use` on that same mux afterward panics. The checked example exercises that failure deliberately, so it cannot be mistaken for a silent no-op.

For a smaller scope, use `Group` or `With`:

```go
r := chi.NewRouter()
r.Use(outer)
r.Group(func(g chi.Router) {
    g.Use(groupOnly)
    g.With(endpointOnly).Get("/report", handler)
})
```

The example records entry and exit in middleware that wraps `next.ServeHTTP`. One request produces:

```text
outer-in
group-in
inline-in
handler
inline-out
group-out
outer-out
```

The last wrapper entered is the first one exited. Place work before `next.ServeHTTP` when it must happen before the handler, and after it when it needs the downstream result. The trace is produced by a runnable test against the pinned source.

`Group` supplies a fresh inline router with its own middleware stack. `With` adds middleware for the endpoint chain it returns. Neither requires replacing `net/http`'s handler interface.

Useful reference points include `Middlewares`, `Chain`, `ChainHandler`, `Mux.Use`, `Mux.With`, `Mux.Group`, and `middleware.RequestID`. Their exact signatures and comments are in the Go API tab, with pinned locations in the [source map](/chi-field-guide/source-map.html).

# A deadline needs a cooperating handler {#a-deadline-needs-a-cooperating-handler}


`middleware.Timeout` adds a deadline to the request context. The handler still needs to stop when the context is done. The middleware does not kill a goroutine or interrupt arbitrary work.

```go
r := chi.NewRouter()
r.Use(middleware.Timeout(50 * time.Millisecond))
r.Get("/slow", func(w http.ResponseWriter, req *http.Request) {
    select {
    case <-req.Context().Done():
        return
    case <-workFinished:
        fmt.Fprint(w, "finished")
    }
})
```

The example follows the upstream middleware's documented pattern. In real code, pass the request context through to context-aware database or HTTP calls. Once a successful response has already been written, the middleware cannot replace it with a fresh status code.

The guide's timeout test blocks only on `req.Context().Done()`, observes `context.DeadlineExceeded`, and returns without writing a response. The middleware then emits 504. It checks cancellation and the resulting response; it does not claim a wall-clock guarantee for an uncooperative handler.

The pinned implementation is [`middleware/timeout.go`](https://github.com/go-chi/chi/blob/9f8adb1aabaa8a91180a821111d3f8e668d1c0bf/middleware/timeout.go#L32). Read `Timeout`, `Recoverer`, and `RequestID` in the Go API tab when composing a service's request stack. Recovery and request IDs address different parts of the request lifecycle; neither makes background work cancellable.

# Coverage and checks {#coverage-and-checks}


Sourcey 3.8.3 extracted **129 source-mapped public declarations** from two packages at the pinned chi commit. This includes **57 functions, 20 types and 45 methods**, plus constants and variables. The snapshot preserves package comments, signatures, type declarations and source positions. The [source map](/chi-field-guide/source-map.html) links all counted declarations to their original files. The machine-readable inventory is committed as `data/coverage.json`.


## Checked behavior {#checked-behavior}


The original Go examples check four path-and-method cases, implicit HEAD handling through a real local HTTP server, explicit HEAD precedence, the observable middleware entry/exit order, a late `Use` panic, and cooperative context cancellation with a 504 response. These are bounded examples of the three recipes, rather than a claim that this guide re-tests chi's entire implementation.

The site verifier checks generated HTML and local fragments, source-map commit pins, and that every counted declaration's anchor is present in the generated reference. See [reproduce](/chi-field-guide/reproduce.html) for the commands.


## Limits {#limits}


The public surface is a snapshot of one commit. It does not cover upstream example modules or private helpers, and it does not establish compatibility with future chi releases. The initial Sourcey snapshot contains no extracted upstream examples; the guide supplies and runs its own examples separately rather than calling that field covered. Browser appearance, source extraction, link checks and executed Go behavior are separate checks.

For current upstream changes, consult [go-chi/chi](https://github.com/go-chi/chi). This independent guide records its exact source revision.

# Reproduce this version {#reproduce-this-version}


The documentation and the examples share one upstream revision: `9f8adb1aabaa8a91180a821111d3f8e668d1c0bf` of `go-chi/chi`. The source module requires Go 1.24; the recorded extraction and examples use Go 1.27.3. Sourcey is pinned to 3.8.3 in the lockfile.


## Rebuild the committed documentation {#rebuild-the-committed-documentation}


```sh
npm ci --ignore-scripts --no-audit --no-fund
npm run build
npm run verify
```

The committed `data/godoc.json` was emitted by Sourcey's Go introspector. Snapshot mode builds the same documented declarations without installing Go on the documentation host.


## Regenerate from source {#regenerate-from-source}


```sh
node scripts/fetch-upstream.mjs
npm run snapshot
cd examples
go test -v ./...
```

The fetch step fails if the checkout does not resolve to the pinned commit. The snapshot step invokes Sourcey's `godoc` command with examples enabled. Timestamps in the snapshot describe extraction time; a new extraction may change that timestamp even when declarations do not change.


## What is verified {#what-is-verified}


The site check inventories generated HTML, tests internal file and fragment targets, checks that the expected exported symbols appear in the reference, and verifies that source-map links use the pinned commit. The Go tests exercise observable HTTP behavior in the three recipes. [Coverage](/chi-field-guide/coverage.html) lists the extracted surface and its limits.

The public source repository keeps configuration, original recipes, tests, the raw Go snapshot, the upstream license and reproducible scripts. The published site is static HTML generated by Sourcey.

documents.searchText:
Package chi is a small, idiomatic and composable router for building HTTP services.

chi supports the four most recent major versions of Go.

### Example

	package main

	import (
		"net/http"

		"github.com/go-chi/chi/v5"
		"github.com/go-chi/chi/v5/middleware"
	)

	func main() {
		r := chi.NewRouter()
		r.Use(middleware.Logger)
		r.Use(middleware.Recoverer)

		r.Get("/", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
			w.Write([]byte("root."))
		})

		http.ListenAndServe(":3333", r)
	}

See [github.com/go-chi/chi/v5/\_examples](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/go-chi/chi/v5/_examples) for more in-depth examples.

### URL patterns

URL patterns allow for easy matching of path components in HTTP requests. The matching components can then be accessed using [chi.URLParam](#func-URLParam)(). All patterns must begin with a slash.

A simple named placeholder {name} matches any sequence of characters up to the next / or the end of the URL. Trailing slashes on paths must be handled explicitly.

A placeholder with a name followed by a colon allows a regular expression match, for example {number:\\\\d+}. The regular expression syntax is Go's normal [regexp](https://pkg.go.dev/regexp) RE2 syntax (see [regexp/syntax](https://pkg.go.dev/regexp/syntax)), except that / will never be matched. An anonymous regexp pattern is allowed, using an empty string before the colon in the placeholder, such as {:\\\\d+}.

The special placeholder of asterisk (\*) matches the rest of the requested URL. Any trailing characters in the pattern are ignored. This is the only placeholder which will match / characters.

Examples:

	"/user/{name}" matches "/user/jsmith" but not "/user/jsmith/info" or "/user/jsmith/"
	"/user/{name}/info" matches "/user/jsmith/info"
	"/page/*" matches "/page/intro/latest"
	"/page/{other}/latest" also matches "/page/intro/latest"
	"/date/{yyyy:\\d\\d\\d\\d}/{mm:\\d\\d}/{dd:\\d\\d}" matches "/date/2017/04/01"

## RouteCtxKey

```go
var (
	// RouteCtxKey is the context.Context key to store the request context.
	RouteCtxKey = &contextKey{"RouteContext"}
)
```

## Chain

```go
func Chain(middlewares ...func(http.Handler) http.Handler) Middlewares
```

Chain returns a Middlewares type from a slice of middleware handlers.

## NewMux

```go
func NewMux() *Mux
```

NewMux returns a newly initialized Mux object that implements the Router interface.

## NewRouteContext

```go
func NewRouteContext() *Context
```

NewRouteContext returns a new routing Context object.

## NewRouter

```go
func NewRouter() *Mux
```

NewRouter returns a new Mux object that implements the Router interface.

## RegisterMethod

```go
func RegisterMethod(method string)
```

RegisterMethod adds support for custom HTTP method handlers, available via Router#Method and Router#MethodFunc

## RouteContext

```go
func RouteContext(ctx context.Context) *Context
```

RouteContext returns chi's routing Context object from a http.Request Context.

## URLParam

```go
func URLParam(r *http.Request, key string) string
```

URLParam returns the url parameter from a http.Request object.

## URLParamFromCtx

```go

```

URLParamFromCtx returns the url parameter from a http.Request Context.

## Walk

```go

```

Walk walks any router tree that implements Routes interface.

## ChainHandler

```go
type ChainHandler struct {
	Endpoint http.Handler

	Middlewares Middlewares
	// contains filtered or unexported fields
}
```

ChainHandler is a http.Handler with support for handler composition and execution.

- `Endpoint: http.Handler`: 
- `Middlewares: Middlewares`: 

## ServeHTTP

```go
func (c *ChainHandler) ServeHTTP(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request)
```

## Context

```go
type Context struct {
	Routes Routes

	// Routing path/method override used during the route search.
	// See Mux#routeHTTP method.
	RoutePath   string
	RouteMethod string

	// URLParams are the stack of routeParams captured during the
	// routing lifecycle across a stack of sub-routers.
	URLParams RouteParams

	// Routing pattern stack throughout the lifecycle of the request,
	// across all connected routers. It is a record of all matching
	// patterns across a stack of sub-routers.
	RoutePatterns []string
	// contains filtered or unexported fields
}
```

Context is the default routing context set on the root node of a request context to track route patterns, URL parameters and an optional routing path.

NOTE: New reference fields (slices, maps, pointers) must be deep-copied in Clone.

- `Routes: Routes`: 
- `RoutePath: string`: Routing path/method override used during the route search. See Mux#routeHTTP method.
- `RouteMethod: string`: 
- `URLParams: RouteParams`: URLParams are the stack of routeParams captured during the routing lifecycle across a stack of sub-routers.
- `RoutePatterns: []string`: Routing pattern stack throughout the lifecycle of the request, across all connected routers. It is a record of all matching patterns across a stack of sub-routers.

## Clone

```go
func (x *Context) Clone() *Context
```

Clone a routing context so that it may be used outside of the request/response lifecycle, e.g. in a goroutine that outlives the request handler.

Clone must be called before the request handler returns; after that, the original context is reset and put back into the pool for reuse by another request, racing with the copy.

## Reset

```go
func (x *Context) Reset()
```

Reset a routing context to its initial state.

## RoutePattern

```go
func (x *Context) RoutePattern() string
```

RoutePattern builds the routing pattern string for the particular request, at the particular point during routing. This means, the value will change throughout the execution of a request in a router. That is why it's advised to only use this value after calling the next handler.

For example,

	func Instrument(next http.Handler) http.Handler {
		return http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
			next.ServeHTTP(w, r)
			routePattern := chi.RouteContext(r.Context()).RoutePattern()
			measure(w, r, routePattern)
		})
	}

## URLParam

```go
func (x *Context) URLParam(key string) string
```

URLParam returns the corresponding URL parameter value from the request routing context.

## Middlewares

```go
type Middlewares []func(http.Handler) http.Handler
```

Middlewares type is a slice of standard middleware handlers with methods to compose middleware chains and http.Handler's.

## Handler

```go
func (mws Middlewares) Handler(h http.Handler) http.Handler
```

Handler builds and returns a http.Handler from the chain of middlewares, with `h http.Handler` as the final handler.

## HandlerFunc

```go
func (mws Middlewares) HandlerFunc(h http.HandlerFunc) http.Handler
```

HandlerFunc builds and returns a http.Handler from the chain of middlewares, with `h http.Handler` as the final handler.

## Mux

```go
type Mux struct {
	// contains filtered or unexported fields
}
```

Mux is a simple HTTP route multiplexer that parses a request path, records any URL params, and executes an end handler. It implements the http.Handler interface and is friendly with the standard library.

Mux is designed to be fast, minimal and offer a powerful API for building modular and composable HTTP services with a large set of handlers. It's particularly useful for writing large REST API services that break a handler into many smaller parts composed of middlewares and end handlers.

## Connect

```go
func (mx *Mux) Connect(pattern string, handlerFn http.HandlerFunc)
```

Connect adds the route `pattern` that matches a CONNECT http method to execute the `handlerFn` http.HandlerFunc.

## Delete

```go
func (mx *Mux) Delete(pattern string, handlerFn http.HandlerFunc)
```

Delete adds the route `pattern` that matches a DELETE http method to execute the `handlerFn` http.HandlerFunc.

## Find

```go
func (mx *Mux) Find(rctx *Context, method, path string) string
```

Find searches the routing tree for the pattern that matches the method/path.

Note: the \*Context state is updated during execution, so manage the state carefully or make a NewRouteContext().

## Get

```go
func (mx *Mux) Get(pattern string, handlerFn http.HandlerFunc)
```

Get adds the route `pattern` that matches a GET http method to execute the `handlerFn` http.HandlerFunc.

## Group

```go
func (mx *Mux) Group(fn func(r Router)) Router
```

Group creates a new inline-Mux with a copy of middleware stack. It's useful for a group of handlers along the same routing path that use an additional set of middlewares. See \_examples/.

## Handle

```go
func (mx *Mux) Handle(pattern string, handler http.Handler)
```

Handle adds the route `pattern` that matches any http method to execute the `handler` http.Handler.

## HandleFunc

```go
func (mx *Mux) HandleFunc(pattern string, handlerFn http.HandlerFunc)
```

HandleFunc adds the route `pattern` that matches any http method to execute the `handlerFn` http.HandlerFunc.

## Head

```go
func (mx *Mux) Head(pattern string, handlerFn http.HandlerFunc)
```

Head adds the route `pattern` that matches a HEAD http method to execute the `handlerFn` http.HandlerFunc.

## Match

```go
func (mx *Mux) Match(rctx *Context, method, path string) bool
```

Match searches the routing tree for a handler that matches the method/path. It's similar to routing a http request, but without executing the handler thereafter.

Note: the \*Context state is updated during execution, so manage the state carefully or make a NewRouteContext().

## Method

```go
func (mx *Mux) Method(method, pattern string, handler http.Handler)
```

Method adds the route `pattern` that matches `method` http method to execute the `handler` http.Handler.

## MethodFunc

```go
func (mx *Mux) MethodFunc(method, pattern string, handlerFn http.HandlerFunc)
```

MethodFunc adds the route `pattern` that matches `method` http method to execute the `handlerFn` http.HandlerFunc.

## MethodNotAllowed

```go
func (mx *Mux) MethodNotAllowed(handlerFn http.HandlerFunc)
```

MethodNotAllowed sets a custom http.HandlerFunc for routing paths where the method is unresolved. The default handler returns a 405 with an empty body.

## MethodNotAllowedHandler

```go
func (mx *Mux) MethodNotAllowedHandler(methodsAllowed ...methodTyp) http.HandlerFunc
```

MethodNotAllowedHandler returns the default Mux 405 responder whenever a method cannot be resolved for a route.

## Middlewares

```go
func (mx *Mux) Middlewares() Middlewares
```

Middlewares returns a slice of middleware handler functions.

## Mount

```go
func (mx *Mux) Mount(pattern string, handler http.Handler)
```

## ClientIPFromHeader

```go
func ClientIPFromHeader(trustedHeader string, trustedIPPrefixes ...string) func(http.Handler) http.Handler
```

ClientIPFromHeader stores the client IP from a single-IP header set by your reverse proxy. Read it with [GetClientIP](#func-GetClientIP).

Only safe with headers your proxy unconditionally OVERWRITES on every request, e.g.:

  - X-Real-IP        — Nginx with ngx\_http\_realip\_module
  - X-Client-IP      — Apache with mod\_remoteip
  - CF-Connecting-IP — Cloudflare

True-Client-IP, X-Azure-ClientIP, and Fastly-Client-IP look similar but pass through from the client by default in those products; don't use them unless your edge strips the inbound value.

If the header reaches us with multiple values (misconfigured proxy that appends, or a downstream proxy not stripping a client-supplied value), the LAST value wins — that's the one set by the hop closest to us, and therefore the most trusted. Fail-closed if the last value doesn't parse: no client IP is set rather than falling back to earlier (less-trusted) values.

v4-mapped IPv6 (::ffff:a.b.c.d) folds to plain v4 and IPv6 zones are stripped before storage.

Overwriting only protects requests that pass through your proxy. A client that reaches this server directly can set the header to anything. Pass your proxy's CIDR prefixes as trustedIPPrefixes to close that gap: the header is then read only when r.RemoteAddr falls within one of them; otherwise r.RemoteAddr itself is the client IP. This mirrors nginx (set\_real\_ip\_from), Apache (RemoteIPTrustedProxy), and Caddy (trusted\_proxies), and Cloudflare's advice to accept origin traffic only from its IP ranges. Without trustedIPPrefixes, guarantee at the network layer (security group / firewall) that only your proxy can reach this server.

	r.Use(middleware.ClientIPFromHeader("CF-Connecting-IP",
	    "173.245.48.0/20", // Cloudflare IPv4, see https://www.cloudflare.com/ips/
	    "2400:cb00::/32",  // Cloudflare IPv6
	))

Panics at startup if any prefix is invalid.

## ClientIPFromRemoteAddr

```go
func ClientIPFromRemoteAddr(h http.Handler) http.Handler
```

ClientIPFromRemoteAddr stores the client IP read from the TCP RemoteAddr of the incoming request — the IP address of whoever opened the connection to this server. Read it with [GetClientIP](#func-GetClientIP).

Use this when this server is directly connected to the public internet with NO reverse proxy in front of it. Behind a reverse proxy, RemoteAddr is the proxy's IP, not the client's — use [ClientIPFromHeader](#func-ClientIPFromHeader) or [ClientIPFromXFF](#func-ClientIPFromXFF) instead.

IPv4 clients on a dual-stack listener surface as ::ffff:a.b.c.d; they fold to plain v4 before storage so one logical client maps to one key. IPv6 zones are preserved (link-local connections may legitimately have one).

## ClientIPFromXFF

```go
func ClientIPFromXFF(trustedIPPrefixes ...string) func(http.Handler) http.Handler
```

ClientIPFromXFF stores the client IP read from the X-Forwarded-For header, walking the chain right-to-left and skipping any IP that falls within one of the given trusted CIDR prefixes. The first IP that is not trusted is the client. Read it with [GetClientIP](#func-GetClientIP).

An unparseable entry mid-chain aborts the walk and leaves no client IP set (fail-closed) — we can't safely trust anything left of garbage.

Use this when you sit behind one or more reverse proxies whose IP ranges you can enumerate as CIDRs. Most CDNs publish their IPs:

	Cloudflare:   https://www.cloudflare.com/ips/
	AWS:          https://ip-ranges.amazonaws.com/ip-ranges.json
	Fastly:       https://api.fastly.com/public-ip-list
	Google Cloud: https://www.gstatic.com/ipranges/cloud.json

Example (CloudFront):

	r.Use(middleware.ClientIPFromXFF(
	    "13.32.0.0/15",   // CloudFront IPv4
	    "52.46.0.0/18",   // CloudFront IPv4
	    "2600:9000::/28", // CloudFront IPv6
	))

The TCP peer in r.RemoteAddr is treated as the rightmost hop: if it is not within a trusted prefix, it is the client IP and X-Forwarded-For is ignored. A client reaching this server directly therefore cannot spoof its IP. If r.RemoteAddr doesn't parse, no client IP is set (fail-closed).

At least one prefix is required. For a single trusted hop directly in front of this server (e.g., nginx on localhost), pass its address:

	r.Use(middleware.ClientIPFromXFF("127.0.0.1/32", "::1/128"))

v4-mapped IPv6 (::ffff:a.b.c.d) folds to plain v4 and IPv6 zones are stripped before the prefix check and storage; otherwise an attacker could use either notation to alias a trusted IP past the check.

If you know the number of trusted proxies but not their IPs, use [ClientIPFromXFFTrustedProxies](#func-ClientIPFromXFFTrustedProxies) instead.

Panics at startup if no prefix is given or any prefix is invalid.

## ClientIPFromXFFTrustedProxies

```go
func ClientIPFromXFFTrustedProxies(numTrustedProxies int) func(http.Handler) http.Handler
```

ClientIPFromXFFTrustedProxies stores the client IP read from X-Forwarded-For, given the exact number of trusted reverse proxies between this server and the public internet. Read it with [GetClientIP](#func-GetClientIP).

PREFER [ClientIPFromXFF](#func-ClientIPFromXFF) with explicit CIDRs whenever you can — it cannot off-by-one and is robust to architecture changes. Most CDNs publish their IP ranges (Cloudflare, AWS, Fastly, Google Cloud). Use this counting variant only when proxy IPs are dynamic and unpublishable.

numTrustedProxies = total proxy hops between the client and this server. Count every hop in the request path:

	Single proxy (one LB / nginx / Heroku / Fly.io / Render) ....... 1
	Two proxies  (Cloudflare → ALB, CloudFront → ALB) .............. 2
	Three proxies (CDN → API gateway → LB) ......................... 3

VERIFY BEFORE GOING LIVE: send a request from a known IP and confirm [GetClientIP](#func-GetClientIP) returns that IP. If it returns a proxy IP, your count is too LOW — a client can spoof their IP, fix immediately. If it returns "", your count is too HIGH — no leak, but no client IP either.

This middleware reads ONLY X-Forwarded-For; it does not inspect r.RemoteAddr. Guarantee at the network layer (security group / firewall) that only your proxies can reach this server.

If the XFF chain has fewer than numTrustedProxies entries, no client IP is set (fail-closed). Like [ClientIPFromXFF](#func-ClientIPFromXFF), v4-mapped IPv6 folds to v4 and IPv6 zones are stripped before storage.

Panics at startup if numTrustedProxies \< 1.

```go

```

Deprecation marks a route as deprecated, per RFC 9745. [https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9745.html](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9745.html)

Use it from the day you decide to retire a route. The route keeps working, and clients are told to migrate. When you know the removal date, add [Sunset](#func-Sunset). Middleware order doesn't matter.

	rSubdomain := chi.NewRouter()
	r.Use(middleware.RouteHeaders().
		Route("Host", "example.com", middleware.New(r)).
		Route("Host", "*.example.com", middleware.New(rSubdomain)).
		Handler)
	r.Get("/", h)
	rSubdomain.Get("/", h2)

Another example, imagine you want to setup multiple CORS handlers, where for your origin servers you allow authorized requests, but for third-party public requests, authorization is disabled.

	r := chi.NewRouter()
	r.Use(middleware.RouteHeaders().
		Route("Origin", "https://app.skyweaver.net", cors.Handler(cors.Options{
			AllowedOrigins:   []string{"https://api.skyweaver.net"},
			AllowedMethods:   []string{"GET", "POST", "PUT", "DELETE", "OPTIONS"},
			AllowedHeaders:   []string{"Accept", "Authorization", "Content-Type"},
			AllowCredentials: true, // <----------<<< allow credentials
		})).
		Route("Origin", "*", cors.Handler(cors.Options{
			AllowedOrigins:   []string{"*"},
			AllowedMethods:   []string{"GET", "POST", "PUT", "DELETE", "OPTIONS"},
			AllowedHeaders:   []string{"Accept", "Content-Type"},
			AllowCredentials: false, // <----------<<< do not allow credentials
		})).
		Handler)

## Sunset

```go
func Sunset(sunsetAt time.Time, links ...string) func(http.Handler) http.Handler
```

Sunset announces when a route will stop working, per RFC 8594. [https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8594.html](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8594.html)

Use it once you know the removal date, and keep [Deprecation](#func-Deprecation) on the same route. Sunset alone is valid, but clients get no "stop using this" signal. Middleware order doesn't matter.

sunsetAt is usually a future date, and should not be before the deprecation date. After it, remove the route or return 410 Gone. It panics if sunsetAt is the zero time, which is usually an unset value. Pass a real date, or skip the middleware when no date is set.

Each link is added as-is as a Link header, so it must be a full RFC 8288 value, e.g. `<[https://example.com/migrate](https://example.com/migrate)>; rel="sunset"`.

## Timeout

```go
func Timeout(timeout time.Duration) func(next http.Handler) http.Handler
```

Timeout is a middleware that cancels ctx after a given timeout and return a 504 Gateway Timeout error to the client.

It's required that you select the ctx.Done() channel to check for the signal if the context has reached its deadline and return, otherwise the timeout signal will be just ignored.

ie. a route/handler may look like:

	r.Get("/long", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		ctx := r.Context()
		processTime := time.Duration(rand.Intn(4)+1) * time.Second

		select {
		case <-ctx.Done():
			return

		case <-time.After(processTime):
			// The above channel simulates some hard work.
		}

		w.Write([]byte("done"))
	})

## URLFormat

```go
func URLFormat(next http.Handler) http.Handler
```

URLFormat is a middleware that parses the url extension from a request path and stores it on the context as a string under the key `middleware.URLFormatCtxKey`. The middleware will trim the suffix from the routing path and continue routing.

Routers should not include a url parameter for the suffix when using this middleware.

Sample usage for url paths `/articles/1`, `/articles/1.json` and `/articles/1.xml`:

	func routes() http.Handler {
		r := chi.NewRouter()
		r.Use(middleware.URLFormat)

		r.Get("/articles/{id}", ListArticles)

		return r
	}

	func ListArticles(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		urlFormat, _ := r.Context().Value(middleware.URLFormatCtxKey).(string)

		switch urlFormat {
		case "json":
			render.JSON(w, r, articles)
		case "xml:"
			render.XML(w, r, articles)
		default:
			render.JSON(w, r, articles)
		}
	}

```go

```

SetEncoder can be used to set the implementation of a compression algorithm.

The encoding should be a standardised identifier. See: [https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Accept-Encoding](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Accept-Encoding)

For example, add the Brotli algorithm:

	import "github.com/google/brotli/go/cbrotli"

	compressor := middleware.NewCompressor(5, "text/html")
	compressor.SetEncoder("br", func(w io.Writer, level int) io.Writer {
		return cbrotli.NewWriter(w, cbrotli.WriterOptions{Quality: level})
	})

Alternatively, this Cgo-free Brotli module can be used:

	import "github.com/andybalholm/brotli"

	compressor := middleware.NewCompressor(5, "text/html")

	compressor.SetEncoder("br", func(w io.Writer, level int) io.Writer {

## WrapResponseWriter

```go
type WrapResponseWriter interface {
	http.ResponseWriter
	// Status returns the HTTP status of the request, or 0 if one has not
	// yet been sent.
	Status() int
	// BytesWritten returns the total number of bytes sent to the client.
	BytesWritten() int
	// Tee causes the response body to be written to the given io.Writer in
	// addition to proxying the writes through. Only one io.Writer can be
	// tee'd to at once: setting a second one will overwrite the first.
	// Writes will be sent to the proxy before being written to this
	// io.Writer. It is illegal for the tee'd writer to be modified
	// concurrently with writes.
	Tee(io.Writer)
	// Unwrap returns the original proxied target.
	Unwrap() http.ResponseWriter
	// Discard causes all writes to the original ResponseWriter be discarded,
	// instead writing only to the tee'd writer if it's set.
	// Flush calls also do not reach the original ResponseWriter.
	// The caller is responsible for calling WriteHeader and Write on the
	// original ResponseWriter once the processing is done.
	Discard()
}
```

WrapResponseWriter is a proxy around an http.ResponseWriter that allows you to hook into various parts of the response process.

- `http.ResponseWriter: http.ResponseWriter`: 
- `Status: func() int`: Status returns the HTTP status of the request, or 0 if one has not yet been sent.
- `BytesWritten: func() int`: BytesWritten returns the total number of bytes sent to the client.
- `Tee: func(io.Writer)`: Tee causes the response body to be written to the given io.Writer in addition to proxying the writes through. Only one io.Writer can be tee'd to at once: setting a second one will overwrite the first. Writes will be sent to the proxy before being written to this io.Writer. It is illegal for the tee'd writer to be modified concurrently with writes.
- `Unwrap: func() http.ResponseWriter`: Unwrap returns the original proxied target.
- `Discard: func()`: Discard causes all writes to the original ResponseWriter be discarded, instead writing only to the tee'd writer if it's set. Flush calls also do not reach the original ResponseWriter. The caller is responsible for calling WriteHeader and Write on the original ResponseWriter once the processing is done.
